To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the development of diabetes in rats is associated with delayed onset and reduced extent of Ca overload induced damage of the myocardium in vitro and that this resistance to Ca overload-related damage is associated with microangiopathie, altered Ca handling and impaired myocardial function.

the resistance of the diabetic rat heart to Ca overload is due to the prevention of the Ca entry into the myocardium in vitro and to the prevention of Ca overload-induced structural changes in the diabetic myocardium in vivo.
diabetes results in a resistance of the rat heart to Ca overload-related structural and biochemical damage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the mechanisms of the resistance to Ca paradox in diabetic rat myocardium.
the mechanisms of the development and prevention of the Ca paradox in diabetic rat heart and with the possible pathogenetic role of the altered Ca handling in diabetic cardiomyopathy.
the study of structural and histochemical alterations in the diabetic rat myocardium and the effect of diabetes on Ca overload injury in the isolated diabetic hearts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the resistance of the myocardium to Ca paradox is a characteristic of late diabetic cardiomyopathy in rats.
diabetic rat heart is resistant to Ca overload-induced injury.
diabetes protects the heart from Ca overload-related injury, but the underlying mechanisms remain unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

in the late diabetic myocardium, Ca overload is prevented by the mechanisms of adaptation to the altered Ca handling, which are not fully understood yet, and by the mechanisms of the adaptation to the altered coronary perfusion.
in diabetic heart the Ca overload-related injury can be prevented and that the Ca paradox is not a general phenomenon.
in diabetes the myocardium is more resistant to Ca overload-related structural and functional damage.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the diabetic myocardium is resistant to Ca paradox in vitro.
the heart is a dynamic, living, and changing organ that is capable of adapting to a number of different stressors.
the development of diabetic cardiomyopathy is a complex process, which involves not only changes in the myocardial metabolism, but also in the microvasculature.
